title: Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch
summary: Tesla launches $30,000 Cybercab with a $299 monthly restriction catch
detailed: Tesla invited select customers to purchase its steering-wheel-and-pedal-free Cybercab for $29,900 with a limited December delivery window in portions of Florida and Texas.
Buyers must maintain a mandatory 'autonomy subscription' starting at $29,900 or $299 monthly, without which the self-driving vehicle will not operate.
Tesla, Edmunds director of insights Ivan Drury, and regulatory bodies investigating the vehicle are involved.
This matters because it redefines vehicle ownership into a recurring franchise model, raising consumer debates over software-locked features and ongoing operational dependencies.
sentences: Or in the case of Tesla ’s self-driving Cybercab, several.
Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs.
From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab.
“You’ll never really own the car,” says Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds.

“It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”
According to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription,” a monthly fee that will start at $299.
If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work.

For years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services.
Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers new services as they make them.
The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making.
A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.
In some ways, the subscription model is working.
Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, Internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features.
General Motors said it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.
But some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive.
Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car?
If an automaker can add a new feature at any time, can’t they also take it away?
And if they can take it away, what does “ownership” mean?

In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for preinstalled hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” says Drury.
Tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade.

As the company has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service currently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

In exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the company says.
The fee doesn’t cover insurance.
Cybercab buyers will have other restrictions.
The vehicle is for personal use only.

Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly said owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that.
Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent.
The company “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”
